references.text: 5. Moses gives a parallel list of clean and unclean animals that the Israelites could eat, expanding on the laws given in Leviticus 11.
Ezekiel distinguishes between clean and unclean meat, noting that he has never eaten anything unclean, in accordance with the food laws in Leviticus.
Already in Genesis a distinction is made between clean and unclean animals before the flood, showing that the separation between clean and unclean animals was known before the Mosaic Law.
In Peter's vision, he is shown all kinds of animals and told to kill and eat. This vision abolishes the distinction between clean and unclean animals from the old covenant.
Jesus declares that it is not what enters a person from outside that makes them unclean, thereby declaring all food clean.
Paul writes that nothing is unclean in itself, but can be so for someone who thinks it is unclean, pointing to freedom from the food laws under the new covenant.
